forecasts.note: Restated at each quarterly return. The Q4 restatement comes from the annual return itself, so it lands on the outturn by construction — the interesting movement is Q1 to Q3.

forecasts.label: Interest payable
forecasts.note: The council's own full-year forecast, restated at each quarterly return.

forecasts.label: Revenue spending (net current expenditure)
forecasts.note: The full-year forecast of net current expenditure — the running cost of services — restated each quarter against the same measure at outturn.

forecasts.label: Capital expenditure
forecasts.note: Total capital spending forecast each quarter (the capital payments return) against the annual capital outturn. Capital spending not met from grants or receipts is what turns into new borrowing, so a forecast running ahead of outturn is a borrowing signal.

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter
in_year.note: Per quarter, not cumulative. The quarterly return is a lighter collection than the annual one and sums to roughly 92% of it nationally, so the two are shown apart rather than added together.

news_drafts.headline: Ealing: 79.41% of fixed-rate borrowing falls due in 10+ years, within 40–90% limit, for 2025/26
news_drafts.lead:
Ealing Council's full council meeting on 13 October received its prudential indicators (the limits and measures every council must publish to show its borrowing is affordable) for the 2025/26 financial year. They show 79.41% of the council's fixed-rate borrowing is due for repayment in ten years or more.

That sits inside the range the council set itself, which allows between 40% and 90% of fixed-rate borrowing to fall into that longest period. The rest is spread across shorter periods: 6.60% falls due within 12 months, 1.63% in 12 to 24 months, 4.37% in two to five years, and 7.99% in five to ten years. The council reported no variable-rate borrowing in any period.

The shortest period also stays within its limit. The council's range for borrowing due within 12 months is 0% to 10%, and the outturn figure (the actual figure once the year has ended) of 6.60% is inside it. The figures come from the fourth-quarter outturn report on the 2025/26 indicators, which sets the year's actual position against the limits the council had approved.

news_drafts.headline: Ealing auditors clear accounts but audit work slips behind schedule
news_drafts.lead: Ealing Council's auditors anticipate an unqualified sign-off for the 2025/26 accounts—confirming the figures are reliable. However, audit progress has not kept pace with the original timetable. Auditors and council have agreed to narrow testing to material balances rather than all originally planned procedures, with work commencing in late October. The council is rebuilding assurance work from previous years, with additional costs accrued but total impact unknown. The council is also behind on addressing high-risk matters auditors have flagged for action, with outstanding items rising from 11 to 14. Several have experienced substantial delays: voids issues originally due May 2024 are now scheduled for July 2026; Building Safety Act compliance not expected until 2029. The capital financing requirement—the council's accumulated unfunded capital spending—jumped 27 per cent to £1,322 million in one quarter without explanation.

findings.headline: Internally managed investments earned 4.050% average return, 0.040% above SONIA overnight benchmark
findings.detail: The council achieved average investment returns of 4.050% on £411.889m of internally managed funds, outperforming the SONIA overnight index by 0.040%. This was delivered while maintaining a conservative treasury approach prioritising capital security and a restricted counterparty list.
findings.matters: Investment returns directly add to council resources available for service delivery; demonstrates competence of internal treasury management function managing large cash balances
findings.figures: Average return 4.050% vs SONIA benchmark 4.010% (0.040% outperformance); average managed balance £411.889m; year-end balance £290.109m
findings.quote: The internally managed funds earned an average rate of 4.050%. The comparable performance indicator is the total average of the Sonia overnight rate, which returned 4.010%

findings.headline: Council raised no external borrowing in 2025/26 despite capital financing requirement of £1,043m
findings.detail: The council's underlying need to borrow (CFR) stands at £1,043.462m, but actual long-term debt is only £841.973m, a gap of £201m. No new external borrowing was raised during the year. This indicates the council funded roughly £201m of capital expenditure from reserves and internal resources rather than raising new debt.
findings.matters: Signals deliberate choice to preserve borrowing capacity and draw down reserves rather than take on debt; lenders assess councils' debt strategy and spare capacity; peer councils watch debt management choices
findings.figures: CFR £1,043.462m; actual borrowing £841.973m; new borrowing raised £0.000m; CFR-HRA increased from £278.337m to £382.312m (housing-driven requirement)
findings.quote: There was no long-term borrowing raised from April 2025 to March 2026

findings.headline: Investment balance fell by £127m as capital cash was deployed but capital programme slipped
findings.detail: Surplus cash balances fell from £417.056m to £290.109m as the council used money to finance capital expenditure. The council specifically identifies that lower financing costs resulted partly from 'slippage on the capital programme', indicating that planned capital projects did not progress as scheduled during the year.
findings.matters: Capital slippage signals delays in capital delivery and affects both service outcomes and treasury cash flows; peer councils and lenders track capital performance closely
findings.figures: Investment balance decreased from £417.056m (31 March 2025) to £290.109m (31 March 2026); capital programme slippage explicitly cited as contributor to lower costs
findings.quote: lower financing costs attributable to deferred borrowing and slippage on the capital programme

findings.headline: Council has resumed investments with other local authorities, placing £99m with 20 councils
findings.detail: The council approved resumption of investments with local authorities after a period of not using them. The £99m placed at 31 March 2026 represents a policy shift widening the council's treasury counterparties beyond government and financial institutions. The council carries out creditworthiness checks on recipient councils, which are underpinned by statutory obligation to repay.
findings.matters: Shows a deliberate change in treasury investment strategy; finance directors at peer councils monitor how treasury risk is managed and counterparty lists expanded
findings.figures: £99.000m invested with 20 local authorities at 31 March 2026; £0m at 31 March 2025
findings.quote: The Strategic Director, Resources, in consultation with the Portfolio Holder for Inclusive Economy, has approved the resumption of investments with other local authorities

findings.headline: Maturity structure of fixed rate borrowing concentrated at 79.41% in 10+ year bucket
findings.detail: 79.41% of all fixed rate borrowing matures in 10 years and above, at the high end of the prescribed 40–90% range. Remaining periods show 6.60% under 12 months, 1.63% for 12–24 months, 4.37% for 2–5 years, and 7.99% for 5–10 years. No variable rate debt across any maturity period.
findings.matters: High concentration in long-dated debt locks in current/lower rates and avoids near-term refinancing pressures, but concentrates future refinancing requirements; finance directors at peer councils assess this as a deliberate choice that trades short-term certainty for longer-term re-financing risk.
findings.quote: Maturity structure of fixed rate borrowing during 2025/26... 10 years and above 40.00% 90.00% 79.41%

daily_post.headline: Treasury income, described as strategically important to council funding, will decline as interest rates fall.
daily_post.lead: If treasury income is material to the council's budget (as it states), a significant and sustained fall in investment returns will reduce its revenue baseline. The council will face harder choices about spending or new borrowing, or it must actively manage…
